items.title: Wilson "Chembo" Corniel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019
items.q: professional percussionists that were playing with Eddie Palmieri in the 70s, and they seen that I had a little bit of talent so they took me up and cleaned me up and polished

ctx.x: Jazz for decades was mostly learned by finding a mentor and listening, aurally, and now it’s a big business in education, and thousands of books and manuals on how to improvise and all that. Has the same thing happened with Latin music as far as now you can, all this stuff you’re talking about is now written down?

Oh yes. Oh yes definitely. You know because when I was a kid trying to find information we didn’t have YouTube, we didn’t have the internet. I had my album, I’d put on a record and I would hear the conga player but you would hear the dominant hand and you didn’t know what the left hand was doing so therefore you were doing it wrong because you had © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

to see that there’s a certain technique that fills in the whole pattern of a tumbao. All you hear is [scats] see that’s the right hand only. But what’s this one doing? There’s another, there’s the other half that you’re learning. So you start picking up bad habits already until somebody who knows, and I got in contact with these people that moved in my neighborhood, professional percussionists that were playing with Eddie Palmieri in the 70s, and they seen that I had a little bit of talent so they took me up and…
